items.title: Israeli army used 'trembling' 16-year-old boy as human shield in Gaza, soldier testimonies reveal
items.content:
Israeli army used 'trembling' 16-year-old boy as human shield in Gaza, soldier testimonies reveal
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Thu, 11/26/2026 - 11:57
In report aired by an Israeli channel, soldiers described sending handcuffed Palestinian civilians ahead of troops to search buildings and tunnels for fighters and explosives
Israeli soldiers transfer detained Palestinians out of the Gaza Strip on 21 November 2023 (Menahem Kahana/AFP)
Off
Israeli
soldiers have described the widespread use of
Palestinians
as human shields in the Gaza Strip, including one boy who was just 16 years old.
Soldiers described sending unarmed civilians ahead of troops to search for fighters and explosives in a practice they called the "Mosquito Protocol".
The investigation, broadcast by public channel Kan on Wednesday, featured testimonies from several officers and combatants.
They described how Palestinian civilians, arrested at checkpoints and elsewhere, were handcuffed and forced to search buildings and tunnels before Israeli troops entered.
“The need to use the ‘shawish’ was to make the explosive device detonate on him rather than, God forbid, on a soldier,” one officer said, referring to Palestinian prisoners.
“I will always prefer Israeli army soldiers over citizens of an enemy state,” he added.
All the officers interviewed appeared with their faces blurred and were identified by pseudonyms.
The programme had already sparked outrage among ministers and lawmakers before its broadcast, with some calling for it to be censored or cancelled.
Defence Minister Israel Katz said the report could “damage the good name of soldiers and commanders, and even expose them to legal risks in the international arena”. He also claimed it would reveal the army's operational methods.
Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the Yisrael Beytenu party, warned that the programme would be used “to spread blood libels against IDF (Israeli army) soldiers”.
‘Try not to beat them too much’
An infantry brigade combatant, identified by the pseudonym Ron, said he first learnt about the practice after overhearing a conversation in which a company commander told another officer: “Bring me two Yatomim” - a Hebrew word meaning "orphans" which they used to refer to human shields.
“The following day, the interrogator accompanying my battalion came over and brought me these two young men. He told me: ‘These are two people we arrested along the axis. Use them to enter buildings. Try not to beat them too much,’” Ron said.
'One of them was a 16-year-old boy who was trembling. Both were handcuffed, with their hands behind their backs'
- Israeli army officer
A platoon commander later explained that the men were to be used as human shields, sent ahead of troops to "open doors" and enter positions before them.
“That way, if there was an explosive device, it would explode on them rather than on us,” Ron said.
“One of them was a 16-year-old boy who was trembling. Both were handcuffed, with their hands behind their backs,” he recalled.
“Every time before they entered a position, we removed the plastic covering over their eyes, but we did not remove their restraints.”
In June 2025, the United Nations
said
it had verified the use of 27 Palestinian boys as human shields by Israeli armed forces during operations in the Gaza Strip (22) and the occupied West Bank (five).
Ron described the experience as “horrific” because soldiers had to accompany the handcuffed prisoners to the bathroom.
“I'm sure the experience was even more terrifying for them,” he added.
‘We would have human shields instead’
Another officer said Palestinians were selected after their faces were scanned by a device. If it showed green, indicating that the person was not affiliated with an armed group in Gaza, they could be selected for the practice.
Those chosen were usually young men aged between 20 and 30.
Adam, another officer, said that on one occasion, commanders told troops they would not have a canine unit but would instead be provided with Palestinian human shields.
Israeli forces ‘systematically using Palestinians as human shields in Gaza’
Read More »
“At first, we saw a handcuffed Gazan or Palestinian in an area where there were tunnels, accompanied by several soldiers who were clearly identifiable as special forces,” he said.
“It was extremely shocking because, during the first few weeks, we hadn't seen any Palestinians at all. We hadn't seen any Gazans whatsoever.”
Another soldier defended the practice as a way to save soldiers' lives.
“When there is a practice that can save soldiers' lives, and there is some kind of consensus that it is acceptable to everyone, then that is considered preferable to soldiers dying,” he said.
“It is morally exhausting, but it is also clear that extraordinary things happen during wars.”
The Israeli army has long faced accusations of using Palestinians as human shields. The practice became commonplace during the genocide in Gaza and has more recently also been reported in Lebanon and the occupied West Bank.
The Israeli military says the practice is prohibited and has announced criminal investigations into suspected cases of soldiers using human shields.
However, Israeli military investigations rarely lead to prosecutions.

items.title: Anti-Zionist Jews and Holocaust survivors accuse UK government of 'dismissive treatment'
items.content:
Anti-Zionist Jews and Holocaust survivors accuse UK government of 'dismissive treatment'
Submitted by
Katherine Hearst
on
Thu, 11/26/2026 - 10:59
Holocaust survivors and descendants say a request for meeting about the government’s treatment of pro-Palestine Jews has not been acknowledged
Members of the Jewish Bloc for Palestine march in central London, on 27 April 2024, in support of the Palestinian people (AFP/Benjamin Cremel)
Off
Anti-Zionist Jewish activists and Holocaust survivors say they have been “ignored” by the
UK
government, saying that their "dismissive treatment" in contrast to the treatment of pro-
Israel
groups is "antisemitic".
Jewish Voice for Liberation, and Holocaust survivors and descendants - Stephen Kapos, Agnes Kory and Chris Romberg - said that they had experienced months of “unsatisfactory correspondence” with government ministers.
A request for a meeting to discuss their concerns about the government’s treatment of pro-
Palestine
Jews had gone unanswered.
An open letter - which was addressed to Sarah Jones, minister for policing, and Florence Eshalomi, minister for communities and faith - remains unacknowledged a month on.
By contrast, it pointed to numerous meetings “at many levels of government, from the prime minister down, with pro-Israel organisations and individuals”.
It said that the disparity in this treatment is, in itself, antisemitic.
“Ignoring the many Jews who do not conform with the established narrative of universal support for Israel and Zionism is a position that is itself antisemitic, as it generalises about Jews, reduces them to stereotypes, denies them individuality and agency, and may even endanger their safety, by suggesting that they all support Israel's genocidal actions in Palestine,” the group said.
They said that the letter follows six months of “unsatisfactory correspondence”, which began in May.
That was when some 40 descendants of Holocaust survivors wrote to then Prime Minister Keir Starmer, the Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood and Metropolitan Police Commissioner Mark Rowley refuting allegations that pro-Palestine protests presented a threat to the Jewish community.
Jewish activists warn UK protest crackdown will stoke antisemitism
Read More »
“Six weeks later, a junior minister for policing sent us a really anodyne letter just stating government policy,” Romberg told Middle East Eye.
“We had made the point that the only hostility that we actually face on these protests comes from Zionist counter-protesters,’ he said.
“And the letter we got back said, 'Oh, very sorry that you've had this aggression,' but seemed to imply no recognition at all that it was from the counter-protesters."
The group then wrote to incoming Prime Minister Andy Burnham and said that, since then, they have received three letters from the two ministers which they described as being “dismissive in tone” and containing “generalised statements of government policy, much of it irrelevant to the issues we raised”.
They said that the ministers were slow to respond, with one taking two months to reply.
A government spokesperson told MEE in response to a request for comment that they "regularly engage with a wide range of organisations to discuss their concerns and remain committed to working with our Jewish communities".
‘We haven’t even had an acknowledgement’
Last month, the group received a letter from Jones saying that “this government recognises the diversity of our Jewish communities” and expressing commitment to “meaningful engagement with a range of different voices and perspectives”.
“We thought, good, that's healthy. Let's follow that up,” Romberg, a retired British Army colonel, said. “We're not getting anywhere with these letters. We had been waiting six months with all this, so we asked if we could have a meeting in two weeks.”
But the letter went unanswered.
“It's now been four weeks, and we haven’t even had an acknowledgement,” Romberg said.
The statement noted the “complete contrast” in the government’s attitude to pro-Israel groups, saying that they were not aware of either Burnham or his predecessor holding a single meeting with Jewish pro-Palestine or anti-Zionist organisations.
“The approach the government is taking is actually an approach that is itself in danger of being antisemitic,” Romberg told MEE.
'The approach the government is taking is actually an approach that is itself in danger of being antisemitic'
- Chris Romberg, Holocaust survivor descendant
“They seem to want to ignore Jewish groups that do not fit in with their stereotypical view of what Jews should be. That Jews should support Israel. Jews should be pro-Zionist. And when there are groups that do not fit into that narrative, then they just want to ignore them and won't engage with them.”
MEE is aware of numerous meetings in the last 12 months between government ministers and the Board of Deputies of British Jews, the Jewish Leadership Council - both of whom intervened in the appeal of the government's ban on direct action group Palestine Action - and the Community Security Trust.
In the months before the proscription of Palestine Action, Met chief Rowley
met with the Jewish Board of Deputies
on 6 November 2024 to discuss a series of actions by the group.
A government spokesperson said that: "As the Court of Appeal found, Palestine Action is not a civil disobedience protest group but one that carried out acts of terrorism, celebrated those who took part in them and promoted the use of violence."
Declassified has
revealed
that a number of meetings between ministers and pro-Israel lobbyists were unminuted, including an off-the-record meeting between then Foreign Minister David Lammy and pro-Israeli businessman Trevor Chinn in February 2025.
Another meeting between Middle East Minister Hamish Falconer and Chinn a month later was also not recorded in transparency data.
Romberg said he had “very low expectations” that things would shift under Burnham’s government, despite the prime minister’s admission that his party “got it wrong on Gaza” and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s imposition of sanctions on settlements.
“I feel this is deflectionary. This is a recognition of electoral pressures. Words are easy,” Romberg said.
“There’s been a lot of clucking, but there haven't actually been any eggs laid,” he added.

The Saudi-led coaltion had recently renewed strikes on Houthi targets at the city's port, which sits on the Red Sea coast.
Meanwhile, Yemeni government forces claimed attacks on Houthi positions south of Taiz, in the country's southwest.
The government-run Saba news agency reported that Houthi shelling of the city killed a woman and wounded at least seven others, including a child.

items.title: Yemen: Warring sides exchange shelling and air strikes, as Saudi oil facilities burn
items.content:
Yemen: Warring sides exchange shelling and air strikes, as Saudi oil facilities burn
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Thu, 11/26/2026 - 10:19
Saudi-led coalition warplanes have targeted the capital Sanaa, while shelling by Houthi aligned forces killed a woman in Taiz
This satellite image shows large plumes of smoke billowing over Saudi Ras Tanura oil refinery on Wednesday, after Yemen's Houthi military leadership said in a statement that they attacked the industrial facility (NASA Worldview/Handout via Reuters)
Off
Houthi shelling southeast of
Yemen's
Taiz has killed a woman and wounded at least seven others, including a child, the government-run Saba news agency reported.
The news agency reported that the shelling targeted villages in the Sabir al-Mawadim and al-Misrakh districts of Jabal Sabir.
Several homes were also damaged in the attacks, while the injured were taken to hospital for treatment.
A series of air strikes by the Saudi-led coalition also targeted the capital Sanaa, according to media affiliated with the Houthi-led government.
An explosion was reported earlier in the city on Thursday following recent air strikes near the airport.
Forces loyal to the internationally recognised government also said they carried out air strikes on Houthi positions in the Al-Aqroud area of Al-Misrakh district, south of Taiz, following the attacks.
On Wednesday, the Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, as the kingdom’s deterrence and defensive capabilities continue to be challenged.
Riyadh is shooting down the majority of Houthi missiles and drones fired at it, Arab and western officials told Middle East Eye, but it has failed to protect key assets like energy facilities, financial centres and airports.
Houthis say they attacked Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery in retaliation for deadly strikes
Read More »
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has tried to rally the US and regional states to his side but with mixed success.
The US has been reluctant to engage Houthi-aligned forces after its previous failed bombing campaign against them was ended last year.
Egypt, Pakistan, Turkey and Syria have all sent or committed to deliver military support to Saudi Arabia but - with the exception of Syria, which has sent drone operators - the assistance is defensive.
The  Saudi crown prince met
US
Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of US forces in the Middle East, last week. MEE
first reported
the planned meeting, which was the third since fighting with the Houthis resumed in July.

items.title: Egypt prosecutors announce arrest of man over deadly truck disaster
items.content:
Egyptian prosecutors announced on Thursday the arrest of a man accused of causing a massive fire that erupted when a fuel tanker overturned on a packed highway in Cairo, killing 31 people.
The prosecution said the man had "admitted" to speeding when his car collided with the tanker, "causing the steering wheel to slip from his hands and his car to veer off course".
When the car hit the truck, one of its tyres exploded, causing it to overturn, the prosecution said. The fire erupted as a result of a petrol leak, it added.

items.content:
قرائن جديدة تحاصر بارديلا بشأن كتابات "معادية للسامية" والأخير يواصل نفي نسبتها إليه
نشر الموقع الاستقصائي "ميديا بارت" وصحيفة "لوموند" الفرنسيين، الخميس، مقتطفات جديدة من محادثة على فيسبوك، تعزز نسبة تصريحات "معادية للسامية" إلى جوردان بارديلا، رئيس حزب "التجمع الوطني"، وهو ما يواصل نفيه. وكان "ميديا بارت" قد كشف، في سبتمبر الماضي/أيلول الماضي، عن رسائل "تتضمن عبارات معادية للسامية" تعود إلى عام 2013، عندما كان بارديلا طالبا في المرحلة الثانوية وناشطا شابا في "الجبهة الوطنية".

items.content:
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story
here
The Liberal Democrats are saying the UK needs a proper plan for immigration. This is from the party’s asylum and immigration spokesperson,
Paul Kohler
.
Britain needs to regain control of its immigration system after the chaos of Brexit. Yet sixteen years after David Cameron’s ‘tens of thousands’ pledge, six prime ministers and ten home secretaries have overseen wild swings in immigration numbers with net migration now set to fall below zero.
Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services.
The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government. We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by parliament, at a far lower level.
British and European people are leaving in their droves because of Labour’s high taxes whilst non-EU immigration remains far too high. British families are left to pay for it with lower wages, longer waits for a GP appointment and homes they cannot afford. Mass low-skilled immigration must end completely as it is bad for our economy and corrosive to our society.

This dangerous practice risked leading to irreversible miscarriages of justice, as Israel moved to implement a racist new
death penalty law
that targets Palestinians, the report said.

items.title: Why solidarity with Gaza failed to stop the genocide
items.content:
Why solidarity with Gaza failed to stop the genocide
Submitted by
Ghada Majadli
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 12:01
We need to think more seriously about how solidarity can become an ongoing political commitment rather than a reaction to particular moments of violence
Abeer, the wife of Khaled Naeem, who was killed in an Israeli strike, mourns together with her son and daughter in Gaza City on 21 November 2026 (AFP)
Off
On 12 November,
Israel
attacked Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, killing six Palestinians and injuring dozens more.
Among
those killed
were Saif Abu Hatab, who was awaiting surgery, and Dr Rizq Abu Shaeira, a
surgeon
working at the hospital. Other surgeons, patients and their companions were among the injured.
Beyond the reporting and familiar condemnations from human rights organisations and UN agencies, the attack appeared to provoke little reaction, let alone meaningful political consequences for Israel.
But is this really surprising?
After Israel
systematically
attacked and dismantled Gaza's healthcare system from 2023 through 2025, why would another attack on another hospital warrant a different response?
Still, this is precisely the moment to ask some serious questions about the international political order and its response to
Israel's genocide in Gaza
.
How have we reached a point where an attack on a hospital, killing patients and the doctors treating them, can pass almost unnoticed?
Growing indifference
Three years into the genocide, the growing numbness and indifference towards Gaza are increasingly difficult to ignore. Since the ceasefire came into effect in October 2025, more than 1,600 Palestinians have reportedly been killed and 5,833 injured, while the humanitarian situation remains catastrophic.
Israel is continuing the genocide - but the UK media will not tell you
Read More »
Much of Gaza lies in ruins, its healthcare system devastated, and hundreds of thousands of Palestinians remain displaced. With winter arriving, heavy rains have
flooded
displacement camps, leaving families who have already lost their homes
struggling to find
somewhere dry and safe to sleep.
None of this was unexpected, yet Israel's
continuous restrictions
on essential supplies and the destruction of infrastructure have left people exposed to conditions that could have been prevented.
What is particularly disturbing is that Palestinians are now enduring these conditions with even less international attention than before.
The ceasefire has helped create the impression that the worst is over, allowing governments and political leaders to speak of rehabilitation and peace despite the continued destruction of Palestinian life.
Against the backdrop of
the Israeli elections
, political attention has increasingly shifted towards Israel's domestic politics, electoral alliances and the possibility of replacing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
For many, the prospect of removing the government responsible for so much destruction offers a sense of hope and political urgency. And while a change of government could bring some relief, there is a danger in treating it as a turning point for Palestinians.
The siege of Gaza did not begin with Netanyahu, Ben Gvir or Smotrich, nor did the occupation and dispossession of Palestinians.
These policies have been pursued and maintained by successive Israeli governments, including those presented as more moderate. Yet, as the debate increasingly centres on who will govern Israel next, the question of what will change for the Palestinians, and particularly for those in Gaza, risks being pushed aside.
The growing indifference towards Gaza cannot be understood simply as a consequence of declining media attention or public exhaustion.
During the first year of the genocide, millions of people took to the streets, students established
encampments
, workers
organised,
and campaigns demanding an end to military and institutional ties with Israel gained momentum.
Gaza was at the centre of global attention, and the evidence of Israel's atrocities was impossible to ignore. Yet, none of this brought the genocide to an end.
No concrete change
This is a reality we need to confront. The problem cannot simply be that people are no longer paying attention.
For a considerable period, they were paying attention, protesting and demanding action. And still, Israel continued its attacks and destruction, with the political and military support of some of the world's most powerful governments.
Gaza was at the centre of global attention, and the evidence of Israel's atrocities was impossible to ignore. Yet, none of this brought the genocide to an end
This is not to dismiss the significance of these mobilisations. Steps have indeed been taken within universities, trade unions and other institutions to challenge their complicity and
cut ties with Israel
.
Some campaigns have secured concrete changes, while others continue to organise towards goals that may take years to achieve.
Political struggles do not produce all their outcomes overnight, nor should their significance be measured solely by immediate results.
But acknowledging these achievements should not prevent us from recognising the enormous gap between the scale of global mobilisation and the reality facing Palestinians in Gaza.
Three years into the genocide, despite extensive documentation of atrocities, mass public opposition to the genocide and international legal proceedings, Israel has not faced consequences sufficient to stop the violence, and meanwhile, trucks carrying tents, blankets, mattresses and other essential supplies remain
stranded
outside Gaza, as Israeli restrictions continue to obstruct their entry.
This should trouble us profoundly, not because the mobilisations have been meaningless, but because of what their inability to stop the genocide reveals about the broader political and economic order that has enabled it to continue.
The problem is not that the world has failed to understand what is happening in Gaza. It is that this knowledge has not translated into the political will to stop it.
What is particularly alarming is how quickly Gaza fades from public attention when Palestinians are no longer being killed in large numbers, even as the conditions that have made such violence possible remain unchanged.
Mass killing cannot be the only catalyst for outrage and mobilisation, nor can our attention to Gaza depend on the scale of Palestinian suffering at any given moment.
Ongoing political commitment
This brings us to another difficult question: what does solidarity with Gaza look like after three years of genocide, political exhaustion and mobilisation that, despite its scale, has failed to bring an end to the violence?
And how can it be sustained when Palestinians are no longer being killed in the hundreds in a single day, but continue to die from frequent Israeli air strikes, the collapse of healthcare and the destruction of the basic conditions necessary for life?
Palestinians should not have to experience another massacre to bring people back into the streets. Nor should solidarity depend on a constant supply of images and testimonies of death and destruction.
While some of us have the privilege of turning away, Palestinians in Gaza must continue living through what the rest of the world can choose to stop watching
The past three years have demonstrated the limitations of a politics that relies on shock and bursts of outrage to sustain itself.
This is not an argument against demonstrations, but an invitation to think more seriously about how solidarity can become an ongoing political commitment rather than a reaction to particular moments of violence.
How do we organise for changes that may take years, while refusing to accept that Palestinians should have to wait years for their lives to be protected? How do we sustain political pressure while confronting the limitations of the strategies pursued so far?
These questions have no easy answers. But they are precisely the questions we need to confront, rather than waiting for another massacre to return Gaza to the centre of public attention. Solidarity cannot be reduced to witnessing Palestinian suffering.
It must also engage with Palestinian political demands and challenge the conditions that have made this destruction possible.
The attack on Nasser Hospital should have been intolerable. So should the continued killing of Palestinians after the ceasefire and the flooding of displacement camps.
Exhaustion is understandable, particularly after three years of witnessing such immense suffering. But exhaustion is not experienced equally.
While some of us have the privilege of turning away, Palestinians in Gaza must continue living through what the rest of the world can choose to stop watching.
Perhaps solidarity also means recognising this unequal burden, and asking how those of us with greater safety and freedom can take on more of the responsibility for sustaining political attention and action, even when the urgency of the moment has faded.
Three years into the genocide, perhaps the question is no longer simply how to bring Gaza back to the world's attention, but how to sustain a politics of solidarity that does not depend on that attention in the first place.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Eye.
Israel's genocide in Gaza

items.title: Yemen war: How do the rival alliances and armed factions stack up?
items.content:
Yemen war: How do the rival alliances and armed factions stack up?
Submitted by
Daniel Tester
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 15:50
The Saudi-backed government is leading a fragile coalition including the Giants Brigades, Homeland Shield and other military units against the Iran-aligned Houthis
A fighter, left, loyal to Yemen's government in western Taiz province; and right, a fighter loyal to the Houthi authorities, in Sanaa (both AFP, October 2026)
Off
Yemen
, where civil war broke out in 2014, has recently been rocked by the worst fighting in years. A truce agreed in 2022 between the Ansar Allah, better known as the Houthis,
who control the north, and forces loyal to the government in the south disintegrated when
Saudi Arabia
bombed Sanaa
airport
in July.
In August and September, the Houthis mounted a quick offensive, recapturing much of the western coast, including the port of Mocha, putting it within close range of ships passing the strategically important Bab el-Mandab strait.
The Houthis are now targeting Aden, Yemen’s second city and seat of its internationally recognised government since the group took the capital Sanaa 12 years ago.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have tightened their decade-long siege of Taiz, blocking the road to Aden and raising the prospect of its capture.
The Saudi-backed pro-government military coalition contains a variety of armed units and local militias, each with different goals, rival leaders and origins, leading to infighting and disorganisation.
Allegiances frequently shift and evolve: the Giants Brigade and the National Resistance Forces were each previously backed by the
UAE
. The leaders of both, like much of the coalition, are now bankrolled by Riyadh amid its fallout with Abu Dhabi.
With fighting spread across multiple front lines, here’s an overview of the most important military and political parties involved in the conflict.
The Presidential Leadership Council alliance
Yemen has been officially administered by the eight-member
Presidential Leadership Council (PLC)
since 2022, chaired by politician Rashad al-Alimi. It is recognised internationally as the government of Yemen, and backed by Saudi Arabia.
Several PLC members lead their own military units, which nominally make up Yemen’s armed forces but are ultimately accountable to their commanders and their external backers.
The Giants Brigades
(Al-Amaliqa), mostly drawn from southern Salafi and tribal fighters, are estimated to number 20,000–30,000 fighters. Their leader is Abdulrahman al-Muharrami, better known as Abu Zaraa, a Salafi cleric turned military commander from Lahij governorate who sits on the PLC.
The units were originally armed, trained and funded by the UAE and were long affiliated with the STC, but have been on the Riyadh payroll since Abu Dhabi pulled back from Yemen earlier this year.
Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King's College London's School of Security Studies, told Middle East Eye that "Riyadh has been able to co-opt individuals such as Abu Zaraa, but it has not been able to absorb their entire networks. The Giants retain their southern identity and longstanding Emirati relationships."
The force is among the coalition's best-equipped: it was key to the recapture of the western coast from the Houthis in 2017 (albeit with aerial support from the UAE), and is integral to the current government's defence of Aden.
Many of the Giants’ fighters identify as southerners and are reluctant to defend territory beyond southern Yemen.
Islah
(formally known as the Yemeni Congregation for Reform) is a Sunni political movement with historic ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. It also includes Salafi and tribal fighters.
Despite its ideological affiliations, it is crucial to Riyadh's political and military network in Yemen. The UAE, however, has long opposed Islah, and has
lobbied
abroad for it to be classified as a terrorist group.
Islah is especially influential in Taiz, where it dominates the government's security operation, including the Taiz Military Axis, which coordinates the military units defending the city against 11 years of Houthi siege.
Homeland Shield
(Quwat Dira al-Watan, also known in English as the National Shield Forces) is led by commander Abdulrahman al-Lahji.
It was established in 2022 and formalised as a military unit the following year with the backing of PLC chair Rashad al-Alimi. Its estimated 30-40,000 fighters principally come from Salafi and tribal communities in the eastern Hadramaut and al-Mahrah governorates.
Homeland Shield was key to the recapture of Hadramaut from the STC-affiliated forces in January and is now fighting the Houthis along the eastern frontline. It has also been used as a police force to quell internal discontent, including in
crackdowns
on rallies of STC supporters.
The
National Resistance Forces
are led by Tareq Saleh, nephew and former aide of President Ali Abdullah Saleh, who was driven from power in 2012 and killed by the Houthis, his onetime allies, in 2018.
Many of its fighters come from the remnants of the former president's Republican Guard, who were
backed
by the UAE until the STC’s failed putsch in January. It has subsequently
shifted allegiances
- and its payroll - to Riyadh. Unlike the UAE-backed STC, it nominally supports a unified Yemen.
A Giants Brigades fighter fires from the back of a pickup truck during clashes with Houthis in Taiz province in October 2026 (handout/AFP)
From its HQ in Mocha, the NRF’s estimated 50,000 fighters controlled much of the Red Sea coastline until their position collapsed dramatically amid the Houthis’ August-September offensive. Saleh fled to Riyadh on 12 September, and some NRF troops have since been redeployed to remote regions of Hadramaut.
Krieg said that the loss of Mocha meant that the NRF had lost "its principal territorial, logistical and political base," leaving the force "severely degraded. The forces retain experienced personnel, but I would no longer regard the NRF as a credible independent offensive force in the short term."
The
Hadramaut Tribal Alliance (HTA)
is a coalition that wants greater autonomy for the governorate, home to much of Yemen’s modest oil reserves and where there has long been resentment against Aden’s political and military control.
Founded in 2015, its leader is tribal sheikh Amr bin Habrish, who has called for greater local control over natural resources, security forces and politics. Its armed wing, the Hadramaut Protection Forces, sits outside government control but has been courted by Riyadh to counter UAE-backed southern fighters.
In December 2025, the HTA tried to take Hadramaut’s oil fields, sparking the STC’s failed putsch later that month. Bin Habrish travelled to Saudi Arabia in January amid clashes between his forces and the UAE-backed STC. In July, Saudi authorities prevented him from returning to Yemen without explanation.
The Houthis and allies
The rebel alliance is dominated by the
Houthis
or Ansar Allah ("helpers of God"), which emerged from the Saada governorate in northern Yemen during the 1990s.
It currently has an estimated 350,000 fighters, wants international recognition as the government of Yemen, and an end to the ongoing Saudi blockade, which has caused devastating
hunger
. The group is rooted in Zaydism, a minority branch of Shia Islam that is concentrated in the northern highlands.
Amid demands for northern autonomy, the Houthis repeatedly fought the Saleh government between 2004 and 2010.
The group, now led by Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, brother of founder Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi, seized Sanaa in September 2014. Six months later, Saudi Arabia led a military coalition to restore the government.
In 2022, a UN-brokered informal ceasefire left the Houthis with 30 percent of Yemen, containing 80 percent of the population.
Houthi supporters raise their rifles as they chant slogans during an anti-Israel rally in solidarity with Gaza and Lebanon in Sanaa, Yemen, in October 2024 (AFP)
The group has received extensive military and tactical support from
Iran
, including shipments that allow them to build some of Tehran’s most
sophisticated missile and drone systems
. It has also received support from
Hezbollah
. Although the Houthis claim to be Yemen's government, they are only recognised as such by Iran.
The group, whose slogan is “God is the greatest, death to America, death to
Israel
, curse the Jews, victory to Islam", has attacked Israel since October 2023, as well as vessels linked to Israel and Saudi Arabia that navigate the Bab el-Mandab strait. The Houthis have also repeatedly hit Saudi Arabia, including
Riyadh’s airport
.
Throughout its decade running northern Yemen, the Houthis have forged alliances with local tribal leaders, but have also faced
discontent
from local sheikhs and tribal groups that have been strong-armed by the Houthi leadership in Sanaa.
The Southern Transitional Council
The Southern Transitional Council (STC) is no longer the force it was 12 months ago but its influence is still felt. It was a political body that emerged in April 2017 amid longstanding calls for a separate southern Yemeni state, which
existed
between 1967 and 1990.
During the war, it had the political and financial backing of the UAE, which helped it
seize
Aden in 2019 and become the dominant power across much of the south. It was allied with the government against the Houthis: three STC leaders, including founder Aidarous al-Zubaidi, held seats on the PLC.
In December 2025, its Hadrami Elite Forces seized territory in Hadramaut and al-Mahra governorates, which would have given it control over almost all of the former state of South Yemen.
Fighters of the UAE-trained Security Belt Force, dominated by members of the Southern Transitional Council, ride atop a tank in Shuqrah, east of Aden, on 27 August 2019 (AFP)
This sparked fury from Riyadh, which launched air strikes against the STC and backed a counteroffensive led by the Homeland Shield and others. STC forces retreated and were then forced to disband. Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi, was forced to leave the PLC and charged with treason. The UAE pulled all resources from Yemen, cutting military funding as well as its provision of public services, including hospitals.
The STC now lacks its previous military and political power. Many of its affiliated fighters are now allied with the pro-government bloc and paid by Saudi Arabia.
But support for the goal of an independent South Yemen remains strong in Aden and surrounding areas, where there have been pro-STC
protests
, prompting violent crackdowns from pro-government security forces. The group has also
reopened
branches across the country.
"The Saudis succeeded in dismantling much of the STC’s institutional architecture in January, but they have not dismantled the social, political and military networks on which it was built," Krieg says.
"The southern question remains unresolved, and Saudi Arabia’s inability to deliver security, economic stability and effective governance has arguably reinvigorated southern separatism."
Al-Qaeda in the Arab Peninsula
Al-Qaeda in the Arab Peninsula
(AQAP)
still has a presence in parts of southern Yemen, despite years of counterterror operations. It wants to establish an Islamic emirate throughout the Arabian Peninsula, and is known for its mass casualty
attacks
on civilians.
AQAP fighters, pictured here at an undisclosed location in Yemen in March 2014, no longer wield as much influence as a decade ago (AQAP videograb/AFP)
But the group is far weaker than it was a decade ago, when it seized and ruled the port of Mukalla for a year, as well as parts of southern and eastern Yemen. Today it has bases in mountainous outposts, from which it conducts a low-level insurgency, targeting southern government-aligned forces.
AQAP hasn't had direct clashes with the Houthis since 2022, with whom it has conducted prisoner exchanges and has been
accused
of coordinating smuggling operations.

items.content:

daily political email

New powers allowing defence officials to use lethal force against suspected trespassers into designated zones could have “significant” human rights implications, a Labor-chaired inquiry has warned.
The committee also raised concerns about a lack of requirements to ensure anyone detained under the new laws had access to fresh drinking water and humane conditions. It noted the broad and extensive changes could capture unwitting members of the public who stumble on to a declared defence security zone that has not been publicised.

items.title: بورما ترفض الامتثال لبنود من قرار محكمة العدل الدولية بشأن الروهينغا وتعتبرها "غير مناسبة"
items.content:
بورما ترفض الامتثال لبنود من قرار محكمة العدل الدولية بشأن الروهينغا وتعتبرها "غير مناسبة"
أعلن رئيس بورما مين أونغ هلاينغ أن حكومته لن تمتثل لبعض بنود قرار محكمة العدل الدولية الذي أدان البلاد بارتكاب إبادة جماعية بحق أقلية الروهينغا. وقال هلاينغ، بحسب ما أفادت وسائل إعلام رسمية، الخميس، إن "بورما ستتخذ الإجراءات المناسبة التي تليق بدولة مسؤولة، لكنها لن تمتثل لمتطلبات تعتبرها غير مناسبة". ووصف الرئيس البورمي القضية التي رفعتها غامبيا ضد بلاده بأنها "اتهام أحادي الجانب"، معتبرا أن مصطلح "الإبادة الجماعية" ألحق ضررا بالغا بسمعة البلاد، وفق تعبيره.

👈 اقرأ المزيد: https://f24.my/CJ8l.g

items.title: Pakistan, Saudi, Turkey to hold Mecca alliance meeting in Islamabad Nov 27-28, sources say
items.content:
ISLAMABAD, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey will hold a meeting on their mutual defence agreement in Islamabad this week, two Pakistani sources said on Thursday.
Foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia and Turkey are arriving in Pakistan to attend the meeting, which will be held on Friday and Saturday, the sources told Reuters.
The three countries signed a joint defence agreement in Mecca in August amid escalating concerns about the increasingly aggressive US-Israeli war against Iran.

items.content:
CMA report highlights inflation-busting annual rises and practices that ‘may not operate in patients’ best interests’
Tell us: what is your experience of UK private dentistry?
Business live – latest updates
The UK’s competition watchdog has called for a
shake-up of the £8bn private dentistry market
, after an investigation identified a “catalogue of concerns” including inflation-busting annual rises and evidence of targets to sell more expensive treatments and dental payment plans.
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said patients faced substantial differences in prices in different parts of the UK and “commercial practices, targets and incentives [that] may not operate in patients’ best interests”.

items.content:
دمشق تبحث تعديلا قانونيا يتيح منح الجنسية لأبناء السوريات من جهاديين أجانب
تدرس السلطات السورية مقترحا لإجراء تعديل على قانون الجنسية الصادرعام 1969، ينص على منح الجنسية لأبناء السوريات المتزوجات من غير السوريين، في إجراء يصفه حقوقيون بأنه إصلاحي وطال انتظاره. وتهدف هذه الخطوة، أن تم إقرارها، إلى تسوية الأوضاع القانونية لمئات الأطفال العالقين بلا هوية، ومن بينهم أبناء مقاتلين أجانب في تنظيم "الدولة الإسلامية" ترفض بلدانهم الأصلية استعادتهم.

👈 اقرأ المزيد: https://f24.my/CJ8U.g

items.title: Kushner: 'The good thing about the war is that Gaza does need to be built. So why build it into what it was?'
items.content:
Kushner: 'The good thing about the war is that Gaza does need to be built. So why build it into what it was?'
US special envoy Jared Kushner framed the destruction of Gaza as an opportunity to rebuild differently rather than restoring it to how it was before Israel’s genocide.
"The good thing about the war is that Gaza does need to be built. So why build it into what it was?" he said during an interview on Mathias Dopfner’s MD Meets podcast..
Kushner outlined a vision for Gaza’s future focused on reconstruction, economic development, and regional cooperation. He suggested that if Gaza can be “solved”, there would be opportunities for joint projects with Egypt, including developing data centres and energy projects in the Sinai Peninsula.
Since October 2023, Israel has killed at least 74,700 Palestinians, leaving much of the territory in ruins and forcing 2.1 million people to live in tents and makeshift shelters. Meanwhile, the Israeli military says it currently controls 60 percent of the land.

items.title: China reserves right to take ‘necessary measures’ after Trump’s new tariff proposals
items.content:
Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’, while Brazil ‘will not yield to this type of threat’
Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU
Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash.
Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. It would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.

items.content:
Project capable of powering 300,000 homes, with Britain having offered more than £770m to rebuild energy sector
Britain will add to its multimillion pound investments in rebuilding Ukraine’s energy system by funding a windfarm project capable of powering 300,000 Ukrainian households.
Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, said Britain would invest £9.5m to build a 200 megawatt windfarm in an undisclosed location to bolster Ukraine’s energy reserves as its war with Russia approaches the five-year mark.

items.title: Loud explosions rock Riyadh as Houthis attack Saudi ports
items.content:
Loud explosions rock Riyadh as Houthis attack Saudi ports
Fresh explosions rocked Riyadh on Wednesday as Yemen's Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, as the kingdom’s deterrence and defensive capabilities continue to be challenged.
The Houthis said that both strikes on the ports “resulted in damage” while the Saudi-led coalition acknowledged that a projectile hit the port of Jazan, resulting in minor damage and no casualties.
The port strikes followed an attack on Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery. Argus Media, which covers commodity markets, said the Houthis landed two successful blows on the facility, one at the refinery and one at the export terminal. The Houthis say they bombed Ras Tanura as retaliation for the Saudi attack on the port of Hodeidah controlled by the group.
Saudi Arabia is shooting down the majority of Houthi missiles and drones fired at it, Arab and Western officials tell Middle East Eye, but it has failed to protect key assets like energy facilities, financial centres and airports.

Loud explosions rock Riyadh as Houthis attack Saudi ports

Poll of parents of young children finds three-quarters think pressure from influencers has increased their anxiety
Parents of children aged five and under say pressure from social media influencers to be “the perfect parent” is making it harder to raise a family, according to a
survey
.
Three-quarters (76%) of those who took part in the UK-wide poll agreed social media had increased anxiety around parenting, while three out of five (59%) complained of “impossible expectations” and “feeling judged”.

items.title: Ministers to create new stalking offence and scrap need for proof of fear or distress
items.content:
Victims’ commissioner welcomes strengthening of law in England and Wales but calls for measures to tackle convicted stalkers
Ministers will create a new stalking offence so that victims will no longer have to prove fear or distress to seek protection under the law, the Home Office has announced.
Under current laws, the underlying offence of harassment in England and Wales, as well as additional factors such as the victim’s alarm, must be established for it to be considered stalking. The new law, alongside other changes, will focus on the perpetrator’s behaviour instead, officials said.
Continue reading...

The word-of-mouth success of the journalist’s investigation into the death of a London teenager is ‘one of the defining features of the literary year’
London Falling, Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestselling investigation into the mysterious death of a London teenager, has been named Waterstones book of the year.
The book follows the parents of Zac Brettler, a 19-year-old who fell from the balcony of a luxury London apartment after pretending to be the son of a wealthy Russian oligarch, as they discover the murky, dangerous underworld of the city that their son had been drawn into.

Children who share a bedroom and lack a quiet place to study at home get worse GCSE results than their peers, according to a major report on how poor housing affects education.
The research, carried out by leading academics at University College London for the Sutton Trust, a social mobility charity, urged UK ministers to ensure all young people in rented accommodation have space for a desk.

items.title: US ambassador to Israel undercuts Trump's announcement that aid to Israel will end this year
items.content:
US ambassador to Israel undercuts Trump's announcement that aid to Israel will end this year
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has undercut US President Donald Trump's assertion earlier this month that he "won't be paying Israel" by the end of this year.
Huckabee, the former governor of Arkansas who is an evangelical pastor and a staunch Zionist - by his own description - said on Tuesday at a conference in Tel Aviv that he's "
not certain
that there will be a cessation on an abrupt basis by the end of this year".
That's because Washington currently gives Israel $3.8bn a year, in a 10-year memorandum of understanding that runs from 2019 to 2028.
The package also includes $3.3bn in foreign military financing and $500m in cooperative missile defence programmes.

items.title: Loud explosions rock Riyadh as Houthis attack Saudi ports
items.content:
Loud explosions rock Riyadh as Houthis attack Saudi ports
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 21:13
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman expected to travel to the US next month for G-20 in first trip since start of war
This aerial photograph shows a view of the Riyadh skyline on 23 November 2026
Off
Fresh explosions rocked Riyadh on Wednesday as Yemen's Houthis claimed attacks on
Saudi Arabia’s
Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, as the kingdom’s deterrence and defensive capabilities continue to be challenged.
The Houthis said that both strikes on the ports “resulted in damage” while the Saudi-led coalition acknowledged that a projectile hit the port of Jazan, resulting in minor damage and no casualties.
The port strikes followed an attack on Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery. Argus Media, which covers commodity markets, said the Houthis landed two successful blows on the facility, one at the refinery and one at the export terminal. The Houthis say they bombed Ras Tanura as retaliation for the Saudi attack on the port of Hodeidah controlled by the group.
Saudi Arabia is shooting down the majority of Houthi missiles and drones fired at it, Arab and Western officials tell Middle East Eye, but it has failed to protect key assets like energy facilities, financial centres and airports.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has tried to rally the US and regional states to his side. Egypt, Pakistan, Turkey and Syria have all sent or committed to delivering military support to Saudi Arabia, but with the exception of Syria - which has sent drone operators - the assistance is defensive.
The crown prince met
US
Central Command chief admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of forces in the Middle East, last week. MEE
first reported
the planned meeting, which was the third since fighting with the Houthis resumed in July.
The US, Saudi Arabia's top military supplier, however has not publicly committed additional support to the kingdom, although it has troops and advisers inside the country.
Iran tensions simmer
Semafor reported on Wednesday that Mohammed bin Salman will travel to the US next month for the G-20 summit in Miami. Diplomats have speculated for months whether the de facto leader of Saudi Arabia would leave the kingdom amid Houthi strikes and the chances of a new US-Israeli attack on Iran.
'Turn on the weapons spigot': Saudi Arabia asks partners for gear to deter Houthis
Read More »
Tensions between the US and Iran have been simmering for months, with the two sides exchanging blows in the Strait of Hormuz and at some land targets.
The US has conducted strikes on Iran’s mainland while Tehran has responded with attacks on US military sites in Kuwait and Bahrain.
Iran said on Wednesday that an oil tanker hit a naval mine and caught fire in a "restricted zone" in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the semi-official Fars news agency.
Brent, the international oil benchmark, was up 2.5 percent on Wednesday, trading at $84 per barrel.
The Trump administration says that it is not interested in resuming the war on Iran for now, and instead wants to use economic means to collapse the government, mainly through a blockade on Iranian ports.
Iran has been hit by debilitating inflation, although regional officials who have travelled to the capital have reported busy restaurants and a sense of calm. Fars said on Wednesday that a substantial shipment of dollar banknotes had entered Iran from a neighbouring country.

items.title: Hezbollah chief demands release of five detained members
items.content:
Hezbollah chief demands release of five detained members
Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem on Wednesday demanded the immediate release of five men identified as members of the Lebanese movement and accused of forming an armed cell.
Speaking in a televised address broadcast by Hezbollah's Al-Manar channel, Qassem said the men had "done nothing wrong" and "must be released immediately".
Security forces had detained the five earlier this month in a mountainous area in northern Lebanon, a predominantly Christian region far from Hezbollah's main strongholds.
A judge on Wednesday ordered their continued detention pending investigation, a judicial source told AFP.
"We are being patient in order to preserve civil peace, but patience in the face of injustice has limits," Qassem warned, adding the group would "push back against danger" if necessary.

items.title: US ambassador to Israel undercuts Trump's announcement that aid to Israel will end this year
items.content:
US ambassador to Israel undercuts Trump's announcement that aid to Israel will end this year
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 18:44
The president's abrupt announcement came on the morning of the midterm elections earlier this month
Students carry placards depicting US President Donald Trump and Israel's caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu carrying guns, as they march during a general strike over rising living costs and military spending called by the CGIL trade union, in Milan, Italy, on 20 November 2026 (Claudia Greco/Reuters)
Off
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has undercut US President Donald Trump's assertion earlier this month that he "won't be paying Israel" by the end of this year.
Huckabee, the former governor of Arkansas who is an evangelical pastor and a staunch Zionist - by his own description - said on Tuesday at a conference in Tel Aviv that he's "
not certain
that there will be a cessation on an abrupt basis by the end of this year".
That's because Washington currently gives Israel $3.8bn a year, in a 10-year memorandum of understanding that runs from 2019 to 2028.
The package also includes $3.3bn in foreign military financing and $500m in cooperative missile defence programmes.
In May, the Israeli defence ministry said that the two sides had begun formal talks to replace the current memorandum, with discussions focusing on joint investment in research, development and weapons production.
The suggested framework was to move the relationship from aid to a more reciprocal partnership.
The Congressional Research Service, a non-partisan research body that advises the US Congress, further confirmed this in a June report that US and Israeli officials were discussing a possible shift after 2028 away from direct military aid and towards joint programmes.
Israel, a full-scale partner
In July, the Republican-controlled House of Representatives narrowly passed a $1.5 trillion budget for the US Department of War, and the bill included a controversial provision that would permanently integrate US and Israeli military tech advancements in a way that would - as Netanyahu
put it
- turn Israel from a foreign aid recipient to a full-scale partner.
Future presidents would not be able to simply withdraw from such a project.
Kushner says Israel is becoming a 'pariah' as his Board of Peace plans stall
Read More »
The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) is must-pass legislation, as it is needed to fund all of the Pentagon's operations in the year to come. The Senate will have to consider it soon.
But emboldened by the incoming Democratic majority in January, a dozen Democrats, led by Maryland Senator
Chris Van Hollen
, are
seeking to remove
the provisions related to Section 219, which establishes the "United States–Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative".
The project would identify jointly developed or Israeli-origin technologies for potential integration into US systems; ensure collaborative research initiatives involving government, private sector and academic institutions in both countries protect "sensitive technology"; and ultimately align military efforts with the Department of War that include the Irregular Warfare Technical Support Directorate, the Defense Innovation Unit, the Missile Defense Agency and the United States Space Command, among others.
Huckabee said at the Institute for National Security Studies conference on Tuesday that American lives are saved "every day" because "we pick up intelligence from our partners in Israel".
Military ties continue
On 3 November, Trump said that his administration will not give its yearly military aid to Israel starting next year, because of a prior understanding he made with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Trump added that weapon sales and other forms of military cooperation would continue.
Speaking on Fox News, the president said that the two had agreed months ago to end the military aid since Israel no longer needed it.
Britain must stand firm against Nusseibeh's UN candidacy
Read More »
“Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4bn a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping,” Trump said.
“We've already agreed that by the end of this year we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it,” he added.
Trump said Israel would be able to purchase weapons from the United States and other countries, suggesting that the change would affect the form of assistance rather than bring an end to military ties.
"They can buy whatever they want. They can buy whatever they want. So can Europe. We make the greatest weapons in the world," he said.
The comments came as Republican lawmakers and establishment Democrats running for Congress - as well as hundreds of statewide races - faced growing electoral pressure over support for Israel ahead of the midterm elections.
And indeed, the so-called
blue tsunami
, led by an energised progressive Democratic movement that wants to curb US aid to Israel, washed over Capitol Hill and state legislatures, including several governorships.

items.title: Saudi-led coalition says it intercepts Houthi drone near Jeddah Islamic Port
items.content:
Saudi-led coalition says it intercepts Houthi drone near Jeddah Islamic Port
The Saudi-led coalition said on Wednesday it intercepted and destroyed a drone launched by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis near Jeddah Islamic Port on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast, adding that no civilians were injured by debris from the interception.
The Houthis said they had attacked the port.
Jeddah Islamic Port is a major Saudi maritime gateway on the Red Sea and a key hub for cargo and container traffic.
A picture taken on 1 March 2022 shows a view of cranes and shipping containers at a loading dock of Jeddah's Islamic Seaport on Saudi Arabia's western Red Sea coast (AFP)

A judge in the US has ordered the transfer of Thomas Markle, the Duchess of Sussex’s father, to California to face formal charges of possessing child sex abuse images.
The move comes after a federal grand jury on the west coast paved the way for the prosecution of Markle Sr, who is currently being held in custody in Florida. He was charged with two counts of possession of child pornography.

Yemeni government forces report more than 650 strikes on Houthis
Yemeni government forces said they have carried out 654 strikes against the Houthis over the past few hours, according to the army’s spokesman.
Majed al-Nuzaili said in a post on X that the attacks included 21 air strikes, 36 drone attacks, 20 rocket attacks and 577 artillery attacks.
The attacks killed or wounded 109 Houthi commanders and fighters and destroyed or damaged 76 vehicles and combat assets, al-Nuzaili said.

items.title: Tortured into confessing: Report exposes abusive Israeli interrogation of Palestinians
items.content:
Tortured into confessing: Report exposes abusive Israeli interrogation of Palestinians
In 2021,
Israeli
police arrested a
Palestinian
man known as R, who after multiple rounds of torture, signed a confession document for a crime he did not commit.
He is one of hundreds of Palestinians featured in a report by the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI) who faced criminal proceedings on the basis of confessions extracted under duress.
The man, whose name was withheld for fear of reprisals, spent months in prison before video footage showed he had been nowhere near the scene of the crime he was accused of.
Before that video came to light, R repeatedly tried to withdraw his confession to the unspecified crime but was tortured by Shin Bet officials regardless.
Read more:
Tortured into confessing: Report exposes abusive Israeli interrogation of Palestinians
Palestinians released from Israeli prisons are examined by medics at the Al-Aqsa Martyrs hospital in Deir el-Balah in the central Gaza Strip on 10 April 2025 (Eyad Baba/AFP)

items.title: Houthis say Saudi-led coalition carries out 105 air strikes in 24 hours
items.content:
Houthis say Saudi-led coalition carries out 105 air strikes in 24 hours
The Houthis said a total of 105 air strikes and missile attacks targeted civilian sites in the capital, Sanaa, and 10 governorates by the Saudi-led coalition in the past 24 hours.
The attacks caused an unspecified number of casualties, a spokesperson for the Yemeni group said.
